prompt: Which statement correctly defines a vector quantity?
options: A physical quantity that has magnitude only
A physical quantity that has magnitude and direction
A physical quantity that has a unit but no magnitude
A physical quantity that can only be measured in SI base units

answer.explanation: A vector quantity is defined in the Cambridge 9702 syllabus as a physical quantity that has magnitude and direction.

distractor_explanations: Incorrect. This is the definition of a scalar quantity, not a vector quantity.
Correct. By definition, a vector quantity has both magnitude (size) and direction.
Incorrect. All physical quantities have a numerical magnitude.
Incorrect. Vectors can be expressed in any valid units, derived or base; unit choice does not define a vector.
hints: Recall what distinguishes a vector from a scalar.
A vector always requires information about which way it points.
solution: A vector quantity is defined as a physical quantity that has magnitude and direction. Option 2 is correct.
teacher_walkthrough: Step 1: Recall the definition: scalar = magnitude only; vector = magnitude and direction.
lesson_anchors: A vector needs a direction as well
exclusions: vector addition and resolution deferred to l11
